analysis.one_liner: Taxes unsold investment gains of households worth over $100 million and spends the money on young children and families.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the wealthiest households continue to go untaxed on unsold gains.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require households worth more than $100 million to pay capital gains tax each year on a share of their publicly traded stock, and every five years on a share of their other assets — even if they have not sold anything. Their total bill would be capped at 35% of their net worth above the $100 million mark. The money would go into a new trust fund for programs that support families and young children, run through the Education and Health and Human Services departments. The IRS would be required to audit every covered taxpayer every year, with extra penalties for understating taxes or failing to report assets.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children would gain if the tax revenue were actually appropriated to the new Family Investment Trust Fund, which splits money evenly between the Education and Health and Human Services departments for family well-being and child development programs. The bill is aimed at the earliest years of a child's life, which its findings describe as the period with the biggest lifelong payoff. Very wealthy households would also gain a kind of clarity: a required annual IRS audit with set penalties replaces today's sporadic audits of billionaires.

how_it_helps.text: It ends the 'buy, borrow, die' situation in which very wealthy households pay little or no income tax because their gains are never realized; the bill's findings cite the 25 wealthiest billionaires paying an effective rate of 3.4% from 2014 to 2018 and the wealthiest 400 households paying 8.2% between 2010 and 2018.

It includes its own enforcement: the IRS must audit every covered taxpayer every year, with a 20% penalty on understatements (40% when an asset went unreported), aimed at the underreporting that wealth-tax critics point to.

The revenue is dedicated to a Family Investment Trust Fund, split evenly between the Departments of Education and Health and Human Services for programs supporting family well-being and child development, an age the bill's findings single out as the period when investment has the largest lifelong payoff.

It includes guardrails that blunt common objections: a cap limiting any year's tax to 35% of net worth above $100 million, an option to pay the tax on hard-to-sell private assets in five annual installments, and loss carryforwards so taxpayers are not taxed on paper losses.

analysis.who_pays: Households with a net worth above $100 million — roughly the top fraction of one percent. They would owe tax on 30% of their publicly traded stock gains each year (deemed sold, whether or not they sell), and every five years on 50% of their non-traded assets like private company stakes. The bill includes a five-year installment option and a hard cap limiting any year's bill to 35% of net worth above $100 million. Treasury would also bear the cost of annual audits of every covered taxpayer.

drawbacks.text: The tax reaches gains on assets that have never been sold, which is the central design controversy: critics of mark-to-market taxation argue it is difficult and sometimes arbitrary to place a value on private companies and other illiquid assets each year, and legal challenges to taxing unrealized gains were already being litigated in the courts.

The bill requires the IRS to audit every covered taxpayer every year, a major new enforcement workload, and leaves the hardest questions — how to value net worth and each asset — to Treasury regulations that would have to be written after enactment.

The bill itself concedes revenue would be constrained: the cap limits any year's tax to 35% of net worth above $100 million, and the cap is phased in over the first ten years, so the largest first-year bills are spread out rather than collected up front.

Money in the Family Investment Trust Fund is available only 'as provided by appropriation Acts,' so future Congresses would have to vote each year to actually spend the revenue on children's programs; the fund does not itself guarantee spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: a small annual tax on the richest fraction of American households could fund major investments in young children, a period the bill's findings say has outsized payoff for lifelong health and development. The costs are real but addressable: taxing assets that have not been sold is hard to value, especially private company stakes, and the bill leans heavily on Treasury regulations that do not yet exist. The bill's own guardrails — a cap of 35% of net worth above $100 million, installment payments for hard-to-sell assets, and a congressionally mandated annual audit — are reasonable answers to the fairness and liquidity objections. The strongest good-faith objection remains the constitutional and design debate over taxing unrealized gains; but as written, the bill targets only the wealthiest 0.01% and would not touch the tax bills of ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the two committees it was referred to and was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 14, 2022 and referred the same day to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in part, to the Committee on Education and Labor.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote (markup), no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referrals.
The bill never advanced past committee, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $100 million in net worth are better off, because they will continue to pay no income tax on gains from assets they have not sold. No committee or floor vote ever tested the proposal's support, so the richest households avoided the tax without their representatives ever having to vote on it.

for.name: Rep. Jamaal Bowman
for.what_they_did: Wrote and introduced the bill, designing it to tax unsold gains of households worth over $100 million and route the revenue to early-childhood programs.

for.name: 13 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Pascrell, Davis, Wild, Norton, Watson Coleman, Carson, and Clarke.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the tax-writing committee the bill was first referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it; the action history shows no activity after the April 2022 referral.

against.name: Rep. Robert Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Shared referral jurisdiction over the bill's child and family spending provisions and also took no recorded action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with 14 backers out of 435 House members the bill never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.industry: Households with net worth above $100 million
industries.note: They would pay tax each year on gains from assets they have not sold, ending the situation where unsold stock and business stakes generate no income tax. The cap and installment options soften, but do not eliminate, the cost.

industries.industry: Private fund managers and holders of illiquid assets (private equity, venture capital, real estate)
industries.note: Every five years, half the value of non-traded assets is deemed sold, so founders and fund holders with paper wealth would owe tax on gains they have not cashed out — though the installment option and the 35%-of-net-worth cap limit the burden.

industries.industry: Early-childhood and family-support programs (Education and Health and Human Services grantees)
industries.note: A dedicated trust fund would make new money available, in equal parts, for family well-being and child development programs — but only if Congress passes the annual spending bills to release it.
